This article describes how GiottoLens works and why, for contributors and advanced users.
Decisions with a recorded argument link to their ADR in `adr/`; numbers are from the Atera
example (170k cells, about 600M transcripts in 853 tiles) in headless Chrome.

## Goals

1. Full-resolution exploration of GiottoDisk-backed data at any size.
2. Reactive pan, zoom and selection.
3. Selections and annotations that come back to R, as cell IDs or Giotto objects.
4. Panels drawn from the same GiottoVisuals specs as static figures.
5. Fully drivable from R, so an agent working in the user's R session can read and steer the
   viewer without seeing it.

GiottoLens runs with an R session alongside it. The data model and data operations
belong to the giotto object and GiottoClass/GiottoDisk; the browser draws what R prepares and
keeps no second model of its own (adr/0003).

## Overview

```
R session                                   Browser
launch_lens()                               deck.gl (OrthographicView, Y up)
  httpuv on 127.0.0.1:<random port>          zustand store: config + selection rules
  /lens/<token>/     viewer bundle           rules -> masks over all cells (typed arrays)
    session/         manifest, cells,        hyparquet + own point decoder (workers)
                     metadata, panel data    Vega-Lite panels (loaded on demand)
    files/           tile stores, whole
    data/            tile stores, by Range
    image/<k>        image files, by Range    Viv layers, JPEG-2000 in workers
    ws               WebSocket <----------->  requests, selections, rules, logs, errors
```

## Serving

`launch_lens()` serves everything from one httpuv server so the IDE viewer panes (Positron,
RStudio) can reach the WebSocket on the same origin. Nothing is copied or written next to
the data: the viewer bundle is served from the installed package, each GiottoDisk tile store
is mounted in place, and per-viewer files (manifest, `cells.parquet`, pushed metadata and panel
data) go to a temp directory removed by `close()`.

Every URL sits under `/lens/<token>/`, with a random token per launch, and the viewer resolves
them against the page, so a proxy that adds a path prefix (RStudio Server, Workbench, a port
forward) forwards one unit.

The server binds `127.0.0.1` on a random port, and the token path is the access check: without
it the server answers only "not found", including to other users of a shared machine. A path
works where a per-request check cannot, because httpuv serves the tile files on its own thread
without asking R. An Origin check additionally rejects foreign pages on the WebSocket, except
behind RStudio Server's proxy (adr/0006). `SECURITY.md` describes the model for users.

## Cells

The viewer numbers cells by concatenating the cell layer's tiles in manifest order: tile `t`
holds cells `offset[t] .. offset[t] + n[t] - 1`. The tiles are the polygon store's or, for a
spatial unit with only spatial locations (spots, bins), grid chunks of about 16k cells that R
sorts the locations into. R builds this table once at launch (`cells.parquet`: centroid x, y
and the ID) and keeps the IDs; the browser loads the centroids into two `Float32Array`s and
never needs a string ID (adr/0002, adr/0010). Consequences:

- A polygon tile row maps to its cell by addition, so colouring and selection highlighting
  of outlines need no lookup.
- All cells are drawn as centroids from the start, whatever is loaded: all 170k Atera cells
  appear in 0.12–0.16 s. Polygon tiles are only fetched for outlines, near outline zoom.
- Metadata pushed with `push_metadata()` is written in the same order, one typed array per
  column (categories as integer codes with their levels), so the browser joins nothing.
  Each column is its own parquet file, named by its content, with no key column: a row's
  position is its cell index. The files are the only copy: R reads the columns it needs for
  rules and `describe()`, and a type change (`set_column_type()`) rewrites one file. The
  browser lists every column from the payload and loads one when it is used (colour-by,
  a panel, a rule), whole, from the session's static path, so no read goes through R; the
  rest load in the background while all columns fit 256 MB of typed arrays. A column whose
  file did not change stays loaded across pushes. At 1M cells and 30 columns: ~35 KB kept
  in R (it was ~450 MB), a push 0.85 s, a type change 0.03 to 0.06 s, a column read in R 4
  to 23 ms; in the browser a column decodes in 25 to 35 ms. Single-column parquet over raw
  typed arrays: raw saves that decode but is up to 12 times larger for codes and integer
  columns (0.6 MB against 7.6 MB), which costs more over a remote link.
- `pull()` and the catalog panel add columns to the same set. R lists what the object can
  pull (names only, from cell metadata, expression, spatial enrichments and dim reductions)
  from the object it loads anyway, and keeps the list until the next load. A pull is one
  `spatValues()` call with a key per source over the snapshot, loaded again in a job, so
  the viewer holds no object; it writes only the pulled columns' files and adds them to
  the payload, where `push_metadata()` replaces it.
- The cell table draws only the rows in view, from the same typed arrays; past about 400k
  rows its scroll range is scaled so any number of rows scrolls end to end. Its rows are
  the other sources' selection, as the histogram's counts are in cross-filter mode, and the
  cell IDs it shows are asked of R a screen at a time, so the page holds no ID list
  (adr/0002).
- Jobs run in a worker process, so R's main thread keeps serving the page. The backend is a
  local mizu pool of one worker, started by the first job and stopped with the viewer; a remote backend (mirai) goes behind the same interface. A job starts from the
  project path and a snapshot name, never a serialized object, and its result is applied on
  the main thread from the `later` loop, unless the object shown changed meanwhile. A
  worker loading its packages makes the first job about 9 s slower; a pull of a snapshot in a
  warm worker takes about 0.4 s.
- Selections cross the socket as bitmasks over this order: N/8 bytes whatever is selected.

Cells without polygons are drawn as a **mark**: a circle, square or hexagon with a size in
data units and an angle (adr/0010). R works it out at launch: bins whose cell metadata has
`array_row` and `array_col` are squares from a fit of x and y against the grid indices, which
gives the spacing and rotation exactly and refuses grids that are not square (Visium's
hexagonal spots); other cells are circles as wide as the median distance to their nearest
neighbour. `launch_lens(mark =)` overrides any field. Circles are sized in data units with a
2 px minimum, so they are dots zoomed out and grow to their true size; squares and hexagons
are drawn by `ColumnLayer`, which has no pixel minimum, so dots stand in until a mark is as
wide as a dot. Selection stays centroid membership whatever the mark.

The launch mark is a default, not a fixed property: `viewer$set_mark()` changes its shape,
size or angle, or switches it to dots, as a setting kept with the rest of the configuration
(`cellMark`) and so restored after a reload. It is set from R only; the viewer has no control
for it, since the inferred mark is usually right. Segmented
cells carry an inferred mark too, off by default; turning it on shows them at their size
before their outlines load. For 660k VisiumHD-sized
bins, the grid fit takes 0.3 s and the chunking 0.1 s; the neighbour spacing, used without a
grid, 0.9 s.

## Selection rules

A selection is one **rule** per source: the spatial view (lasso, brush), the scatter, each
histogram, the metadata filter, pushed panels and R. Rule kinds: `polygon`, `stroke`,
`range`, `categories`, `compare`, `ids`, `union` and `intersect`, each optionally negated.
Sources combine with OR, or with AND in cross-filter mode, where each panel shows the other
sources only. Within a view, a lasso or brush stroke replaces the view's rule, Shift adds to
it (a union) and Alt or Ctrl/Cmd subtracts from it (an intersection with the negated stroke),
the same in both modes; the × on a rule in the rules strip drops one view's rule.

Rules, not cell lists, are the state (adr/0001):

- They evaluate to masks over **all** cells, so a lasso drawn zoomed out over unloaded
  tiles selects what the same lasso selects zoomed in.
- They are evaluated the same way in the browser (`selection/rules.ts`) and in R
  (`R/rules.R`). `viewer$select()` resolves cells with no browser open, and a rule read back
  from the browser gives the same cells in R. The end-to-end tests compare the two.
- They describe themselves: `viewer$rules()` lists each with a summary and its own cell count,
  `viewer$rules(code = TRUE)` prints the `lens_*()` calls that recreate the selection, and the
  rules strip shows them in the viewer.

Evaluation stays interactive at scale. A point-in-polygon test with edges bucketed into
horizontal bands (`ringTester()`) runs a whole-view lasso over 10M cells in 248 ms (a plain
edge loop took 1.5 s) and is nearly flat in vertex count; tile bounds prune the cells tested.
Masks are cached per rule object, brushes build theirs incrementally while dragging, and
range, category and AND/OR steps are single passes (a cross-filter step on Atera: 2.8 ms).
Up to roughly 10–20M cells the browser holds everything it needs; beyond that, the plan is
R-side evaluation (see the roadmap).

## Browser state and rendering

Configuration (layers, colouring, rules, combine mode, annotations, tool settings, panel
layout) lives in a zustand store and changes only through its actions; it can be saved as
JSON. Runtime data (deck instance, caches, loaded tables, in-progress drawing) is kept apart.
Every store change requests a render, batched to one per animation frame.

The configuration outlives a page reload through R (adr/0009). zustand's `persist`
middleware sends it as JSON text when it changes, merged over 300 ms; R keeps the latest copy
as it came and sends it back before anything else when a page connects. R rather than browser
storage holds it because R outlives the page and already restores the rules and pushed
panels, and a save to file can start from its copy (issue #21).

deck.gl compares `data` by reference, so binary data objects are built once per underlying
array. Rebuilding them each render had deck re-triangulate every polygon tile and re-upload
every buffer on each tile arrival: 1.3–1.5 s of main-thread blocking while loading, down to
about 90 ms with the objects reused.

## Reading tiles

Parquet stores each column of each row group as its own block, so reading a few columns of a
tile means one byte range per column per row group. How tiles are fetched therefore depends
on where the browser is (adr/0004):

- **whole**: one request per tile from httpuv's own thread, with no R involved. On the same
  machine the extra bytes cost nothing and a busy R does not stall panning (10 tiles and
  outlines: 0.9 s, R free or busy).
- **columns**: the footer, then only the needed blocks, merged when less than 1 MB apart
  (about two requests per tile), through the Range handler on R's main thread. About 6x fewer
  bytes, for slow links; while R is busy these requests wait.
- **auto** (default) starts with whole tiles on a localhost URL and switches to columns after
  two slow whole fetches, since an SSH port forward also looks like localhost.

Transcript tiles decode in a pool of Web Workers with GiottoLens' own decoder for the three
drawn columns (adr/0005). It reads dictionary-encoded columns as integer indices, looks up
only the rows the zoom tier keeps (every 16th, 4th or all) and maps gene names to gene
indices once per dictionary entry: 2.6x faster than hyparquet for all rows and 3.4x at 1/16,
with identical output. Layouts it does not cover fall back to hyparquet. Codecs: SNAPPY (WASM),
ZSTD, GZIP, LZ4_RAW and Hadoop LZ4.

At zoomed-out views loading is now bound by bytes, not decoding, which is what the planned
coarse tier addresses.

## Images

An image is one TIFF file, page 1: `.image_source()` returns the giottoLargeImage's
`@file_path`, and that function is the only place that decides which file the viewer reads.
R puts the file and the image's extent in the manifest and serves the file alone at
`image/<k>` through the Range handler; the browser does the rest (adr/0008).

The browser opens each file with geotiff and builds one Viv pixel source per pyramid level,
from the file's own structure: SubIFDs (OME-TIFF, Xenium) or the reduced-resolution IFDs
after the first (COG overviews). Viv's `loadOmeTiff()` is not used: each of Xenium's
per-channel files carries OME-XML for the whole channel set, which that loader reads as a
four-channel file. A file larger than 4096 pixels a side that is stored in strips or has no
pyramid is refused with a message, since Viv would read it whole at every zoom (the Atera
vault's DAPI is such a file: 46543 x 28048 in 2-row strips). The extent becomes the layer's model matrix, so images sit in data
coordinates with row 0 at the top, and Viv's zoom offset follows the matrix's scale. A
flipped, rotated or registered image (a giottoAffineImage) keeps its file and raster
untransformed and the transform in `@affine`; R sends that affine with the extent, and the
browser multiplies it onto the model matrix, so the image is drawn where GiottoClass places it
without resampling.

Whether an image is RGB comes from its TIFF tags: 3 or 4 samples of 8 bits whose
PhotometricInterpretation is RGB, or YCbCr (JPEG-compressed RGB, as H&E files usually are).
Its pixel source then has a trailing sample dimension, and Viv draws it as colour, converting
YCbCr in its shader. Any other multi-sample file is a channel stack, not shown yet. Deciding
from the file rather than in R keeps `.image_source()` the only input: the raster R holds
can describe another file (a VRT).

RGB images draw first with normal blending; added, a brightfield image's white background
would wash out everything over it. Each single-channel image is its own
`MultiscaleImageLayer` above them, blended additively, so images add up like channels; overlapping tiles would then draw twice as bright, so there is no
low-resolution backdrop and no parent tile under a loaded one. A hidden image is removed from
the layer list, not made invisible, so its tiles stop loading. Default contrast is the 0.5th
to 99.9th percentile of the nonzero pixels of the smallest level.

Tiles decode in a worker pool (`data/img-pool.ts`): geotiff's decoders plus JPEG-2000 through
OpenJPEG compiled to WASM (260 KB, loaded by the workers only). geotiff's own pool cannot take
a decoder registered on the main thread, and leaves a tile waiting forever when decoding fails.

Measured on the Atera example (four 46543 x 28048 16-bit JPEG-2000 files, 8 levels each,
headless Chrome, browser and R on one machine):

| Step | Time |
|---|---|
| Open four images (headers, smallest level, contrast) | 0.24 s |
| Overview drawn | 0.31 s |
| Jump to full resolution, three images (45 requests, 12 MB) | 0.62 s |
| Decode one dense 1024 x 1024 tile (node, one thread) | 128 ms |

Against GDAL decoding the same codestream, about 1% of pixels differ by exactly 1: rounding
in the lossy wavelet between OpenJPEG builds.

## The R API is the agent API

Every user action has an R equivalent on the `LensViewer` object, so an agent in the user's R
session can work with the viewer as well as the user can: read it (`describe()`, `state()`,
`rules()`, `log()`, `screenshot()`), drive it (`select()`, `set_view()`, `zoom_to()`,
`color_by()`, `set_layer()`, `push_panel()`), ask the user for input
(`wait_for_selection()`) and get results back as R objects (`selection`, `subset()`).

The protocol is request/reply: a message from R with an `id` is answered by the browser with
the handler's result or error. A tab announces `ready` once its handlers are registered, and
R then sends it the saved configuration, the current metadata, rules and pushed panels, so
reloads and new tabs match. Browser errors
are forwarded and printed in the R console. The page asks R in the other direction for the
start page only: list projects and their snapshots, and open one (adr/0019).

## Panels

Chart panels dock beside the spatial view as tabs and splits (dockview-core, adr/0009); the
spatial view itself is not a panel. The viewer's controls dock the same way, one of each, in a
column of their own (adr/0016). The built-in panels are a scatter of any two metadata
columns, a histogram or bar chart, and a density panel that bins two columns into a 256 x 256
image, coloured by cells per bin, with a rectangle brush (adr/0012), all drawn from the typed arrays and linked by the
selection rules; the `+` menu adds more. The density rectangle is two range rules
intersected, so R evaluates it with no new rule kind. `push_panel()` adds any Vega-Lite
spec, including GiottoVisuals' `renderSpec(engine = "vegalite")`, placed by `where` and
`ref`; rows with a
`cell_ID` are linked, and an interval brush named `brush` becomes a selection rule. Mosaic is
not used: linking comes from the rules, and aggregation from typed-array scans (about 1 ms per
million cells) or from R.

A drag of a range or rectangle brush does not scan every cell per frame (adr/0013). The
brushed columns' cells are kept ordered by bucket, so a move tests only the cells near the
edges it swept, and the panels' counts and the selected count follow exactly. The spatial view
filters every cell on the GPU by the brushed columns. The rule is set once, on release. On
Mosaic's 5M-star Gaia sample the panels follow a drag at a median 17 ms frame. Zoomed out,
the spatial view is the remaining limit (about 210 ms a frame): Gaia stacks hundreds of stars
on a pixel, and blended dots on one pixel are drawn in turn; 5M points spread evenly draw in
24–33 ms.

Each panel has a stable id that names its slot, its selection source and its data file, so
moving a panel changes nothing else. R keeps every pushed chart until it is closed and sends
it again to a new page. A panel behind another tab skips selection updates and catches up
when it comes into view. A panel draws its brush from its own rule, wherever the rule came
from (a brush, R, a reload), so a restored range can still be dragged.

## The large-data path

Selections over cells stay in the browser up to about 10–20M cells. Beyond that, and for
queries over transcripts, the work belongs in R next to the files. Bare SQL on the parquet
tiles sets the floor (one 200-vertex lasso, cell IDs returned to R):

| Data | DuckDB (8 threads) | DuckDB (1 thread) | sedona |
|---|---|---|---|
| 170k cells, centroid | 16 ms | 30 ms | 6 ms |
| 170k cells, geometry intersects | 36 ms | 129 ms | 54 ms |
| transcripts, 420M in the lasso | 49 s | 101 s | 5.3 s |
| transcripts, 1.1M in the lasso | 0.53 s | 0.81 s | 0.83 s |

GiottoDisk's `spatRelate()` took 1.4 s (sedona), 1.8 s (terra) and 5.7 s (duckdb) for the
same cell lasso: per-call overhead, not engine time (adr/0007). At transcript scale nothing
returns IDs interactively, so the server path serves aggregates (counts per gene, densities)
and keeps selections as rules.
